conversation.content:
Hello—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks after birth. Today I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten gentle questions about your mood, anxiety, and bonding with your baby over the past seven days. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification anytime. Ready to begin?

First, I’d love to know: in the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even when things didn’t go as planned?

I’ve noticed that when my partner or my mom tries to make a joke, I can smile for a second, but it feels kind of forced. I don’t really laugh out loud the way I used to—nothing feels that funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes a little giggle slips out if my husband does something goofy, but it’s pretty rare and it fades fast. Mostly I just feel too tired or on-edge to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

There are a couple of things I used to get excited about—like my morning coffee or the show we usually watch after dinner—but even those feel kind of flat lately. I still look forward to holding the baby and watching her stretch, but the spark I used to feel for almost everything else is just…dimmer.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more times than I’d like to admit. When she wouldn’t settle last night I kept thinking it must be because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m not holding her the “right” way or my milk isn’t enough. I know in my head that babies just cry, but the guilty thoughts sneak in anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke, or I’ll lie down and picture her bassinet catching fire. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t snap out of it until I check on her—sometimes two or three times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—those waves come out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was folding her tiny onesies and suddenly felt this rush of dread, like something awful was about to happen. My chest got tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to put the basket down and grip the table until it passed. It left me shaky for a good while.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in tiny jobs—one feeding runs into the next, the dishes pile up, my phone keeps buzzing, and I can’t figure out which thing to tackle first. Sometimes I just sit there staring at it all, frozen, until the baby cries and pulls me back into motion.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… even when she’s finally down I lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I might have messed up, or picturing worst-case scenarios. I’ll drift off and then jolt awake an hour later, convinced I heard her cry. It’s exhausting, but I can’t seem to shut it off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like this gray cloud just hangs over everything. I’ll be changing her diaper and suddenly feel like crying, or I’ll look at other moms on social media who seem so happy and think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” The sadness comes and goes, but it’s definitely there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while trying to get her to latch; the day before, I just sat on the couch after everyone left and sobbed for a few minutes. I feel silly afterward, but in the moment it feels like the only release I have.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like wondering what would happen if I just didn’t wake up, or picturing myself taking too many of the pain pills from my C-section. They’re just passing thoughts, no plan or real wish to do it, but they do pop in, maybe once or twice this week, and it scares me a little.

You've shared that the joy and spark you once felt has faded since your baby arrived, replaced by a near-daily <sym>sadness</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym> that make even small tasks feel overwhelming. You described <sym>panic-like episodes</sym> where your chest tightens and dread rushes in, constant worry that something terrible will happen to your little one, and nights spent lying awake with racing thoughts. Although you still treasure moments holding your baby, you also carry heavy guilt and self-blame, and you've been frightened by fleeting thoughts of not waking up or taking too many pills. These feelings are understandably exhausting and isolating, and it's clear you want relief so you can enjoy motherhood more fully.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports rare, fleeting laughter only when prompted and states she mostly feels too tired or on-edge to find things funny, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeable reduction in enjoyment for most activities, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient frequently blames herself for normal infant behavior, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries with physical anxiety symptoms and repeated safety-checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attack symptoms that struck suddenly while doing routine task, indicating frequent and intense episodes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to prioritize or initiate tasks, and immobilized by the volume of responsibilities—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, severe sleep disruption tied to unhappiness: mind racing, repeated awakenings, and inability to shut off anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day," which aligns with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying twice in a week triggered by specific postpartum stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring passive suicidal ideation (wishing not to wake up, imagining overdose) occurring "once or twice this week," matching "Sometimes" severity.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring: 25/30 with Item 10=2 (passive suicidal thoughts). <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> require ≥5 symptoms present most days for two weeks; here we note: (1) depressed mood most of the day (<quote>pretty much every day</quote>), (2) markedly diminished interest (<quote>spark...dimmer</quote>), (3) guilt/worthlessness (<quote>not doing something right</quote>), (4) fatigue (<quote>exhausting</quote>), (5) concentration difficulties (<quote>mind racing</quote>), (6) sleep disturbance, (7) recurrent thoughts of death (<quote>wondering what would happen if I just didn't wake up</quote>). Anxiety symptoms exceed criteria for <med>Peripartum Anxiety</med> as well. Combined score and safety item place patient in the highest risk category per EPDS guidelines. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Request expedited referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy and medication discussion if indicated
3. Develop a written 24-hour safety plan listing supportive contacts and crisis numbers (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
4. Enlist partner or family to stay nearby and secure prescription medications until mood stabilizes
5. Begin gentle daily routine: 5-10 minutes outdoor daylight, balanced meals, hydration, and accept help with household tasks
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding techniques when <sym>panic</sym> surges; consider free perinatal anxiety apps for guided audio
7. Prioritize rest: split night shifts with support person, nap when baby naps, limit screen time after evening feed
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS re-screen within one week to track progress
9. If thoughts of self-harm intensify or plans form, treat as emergency-call 911 or go to nearest ER
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Persistent low mood and anhedonia (most days, “gray cloud,” blunted enjoyment of previously pleasurable activities)
- Daily guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (“not doing something right,” milk supply)
- Recurrent, intrusive worries and catastrophic imagery (choking, fire) → prompts repeated checking
- Sudden panic-like episodes (chest tightness, breathlessness, dread) occurring multiple times
- Overwhelm/functional paralysis with routine tasks; difficulty prioritizing
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems driven by racing thoughts and hypervigilance to infant
- Frequent crying spells (twice this week, sometimes without clear trigger)
- Passive, non-specific self-harm ideation (fleeting thoughts of not waking up, excess pills) without plan or intent

Pattern:
Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, beginning since delivery; cause subjective distress and interfere with daily functioning.

Screening significance:
Findings consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and comorbid anxiety symptoms; passive suicidal thoughts noted → elevated safety risk.

Risk factors documented:
- Persistent sadness/loss of pleasure
- Guilt/worthlessness
- Anxiety/panic
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood
- Overwhelm with infant care
- Self-harm ideation (safety flag)

Next steps for provider:
Complete standardized rating scale (e.g., EPDS), assess safety plan, consider expedited referral for perinatal mental health evaluation and support.
